n: Outside Eden, Adam and Eve’s family begins. Eve’s joyful words may express hope that this son is the promised Seed. The book of Moses adds that they already had other sons and daughters before Cain.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for marital intimacy.
Sounds like Hebrew qanah, “to get” or “acquire.”

n: Abel is born, and the brothers take up the two great livelihoods: shepherding and farming. Abel’s name means “breath” or “vapor,” perhaps hinting at his short life.

f.g: Hebrew Hevel — breath, vapor, something fleeting (the same word as “vanity” in Ecclesiastes).

n: Cain brings produce from his fields as an offering. The book of Moses explains that Adam had been commanded to offer the firstlings of the flock as a symbol of the Savior’s sacrifice.

f.g: Literally “at the end of days”—after some time had passed.

n: Abel brings the best: firstborn lambs and their fat portions. The Lord accepts him and his offering. Hebrews says Abel offered “by faith,” pointing to the Lamb of God.

f.g: The firstborn of the flock—the best and most valuable.
Looked with favor on; accepted.

n: Cain’s offering is not accepted. Instead of seeking to improve, he becomes furious and sullen. Restoration scripture says Cain made his offering at Satan’s urging and loved Satan more than God.

f.g: His face fell—he looked downcast and angry.

n: The Lord lovingly reaches out to Cain with questions, inviting him to examine his heart before anger becomes sin.

f.g: Very angry.

n: God offers hope and a warning: do right and you will be accepted, but sin is crouching at your door like a wild animal, eager to master you—you must master it.

f.g: “Lieth” translates a word for a crouching animal waiting to pounce.

n: Cain lures his brother into the field and kills him—the first murder. The book of Moses reveals that Cain had made a secret pact with Satan to murder for gain.

f.g: Ancient versions add, “Let us go out into the field.”

n: God asks Cain where Abel is, again inviting confession. Cain lies and sneers, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” The rest of scripture answers: yes, we are responsible for one another.
Abel’s blood “cries out” from the ground for justice. God hears innocent suffering even when no human witness does.

f.w: crieth unto me from the ground

n: Cain is cursed from the very ground that received his brother’s blood. Adam’s ground was cursed for his benefit; Cain himself is now cursed.
The farmer will no longer reap good harvests. Cain will be a restless wanderer without a settled home.

f.g: A wanderer and drifter, constantly on the move.

n: Cain complains that his punishment is too great. His concern is for himself, not grief for his brother or his sin.

f.g: Hebrew ʿawon can mean both “iniquity” and “its punishment.”

n: Cain fears being hidden from God’s face and killed by others. Being cut off from God’s presence is the heaviest part of his sentence.

f.w: from thy face shall I be hid

n: Even in judgment, God shows mercy: He places a protective mark on Cain so no one will take vengeance on him. Scripture does not say what the mark was.

f.g: Seven times over—full, complete vengeance.
A sign of protection; its nature is not described.

n: Cain leaves God’s presence and settles in Nod, east of Eden. Moving “east” in Genesis often signals moving away from God.

f.g: Means “wandering”—fitting for a fugitive.

n: Cain’s line builds the first city, named after his son Enoch. This Enoch is not the righteous Enoch of chapter 5 and the book of Moses.

f.g: Not the prophet Enoch (Genesis 5:18-24), who descended from Seth.

n: Cain’s family line continues for several generations, ending in Lamech.

f.g: Not the same as Noah’s father Lamech of Genesis 5:25-31.

n: Lamech takes two wives, the first recorded case of plural marriage, appearing in a family line marked by pride and violence.

f.g: Means perhaps “ornament”; Zillah perhaps “shade.”

n: Lamech’s son Jabal starts the herding way of life, living in tents and keeping livestock.

f.g: Founder or originator of a way of life.

n: Jubal is the founder of music. The line of Cain develops culture and skill, showing that talent is a gift even where faith is lacking.

f.g: A pipe or flute, not the modern organ.

n: Tubal-cain begins metalworking, crafting tools and perhaps weapons. Naamah, his sister, is named, which is unusual in a genealogy.

f.g: A forger or teacher of all craftsmen.
In the KJV usually copper or bronze.

n: Lamech boasts to his wives in a violent poem about killing a man who merely wounded him. Restoration scripture says he killed to protect the secrets of a combination begun by Cain.

f.w: I have slain a man to my wounding

n: Lamech twists God’s protection of Cain into a boast of unlimited revenge. Jesus later reverses this, teaching His disciples to forgive “seventy times seven.”
Adam and Eve receive another son, Seth, through whom the righteous line will continue. Eve sees him as God’s gift replacing Abel.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew shat, “appointed” or “granted.”

n: Through Seth’s son Enos, people begin to worship and call on the Lord’s name. The book of Moses teaches that Adam’s family was taught the gospel from the beginning.

f.w: call upon the name of the LORD

f.g: Hebrew ’Enosh, “man” or “mortal.”
